chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa narrated from Sa'd ibn Isma'il from his father Isma'il ibn Isa who said:
I asked al-Rida (peace be upon him) about the sacrifices of the Jews and Christians and their food, and he said, 'Yes.'

The first point in these narrations is that they do not correspond to those (other narrations) because they are more numerous, and it is not permissible to move from the more numerous to the less numerous, as has been clarified in other places.
And because among those who narrated these narrations are those who narrated the narrations of prohibition that we presented earlier, namely al-Halabi, Abu Basir, and Muhammad ibn Muslim.
Then, if they were safe from all of this, they would still carry two possible meanings.

One of them is that the permissibility in them is only included in the state of necessity, not in the state of choice, and at the time of necessity, the dead animal becomes permissible, so how much more so the sacrifice of one who differs from Islam?
And that which indicates this is what he narrated.

key_terms.اَلضَّرُورَةِ: Necessity (a state where prohibitions are lifted)

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia ruling on the food and sacrifices of Jews and Christians?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Rida (AS) affirms the permissibility of Jewish and Christian sacrifices, yet Shia jurists analyze this through the lens of *ikhtiyar* (choice) versus *darura* (necessity). The text highlights a scholarly tension where some narrators also report prohibitions, suggesting the ruling may be restricted to times of need or specific contexts, reflecting the nuanced methodology of Usuli scholars in reconciling seemingly contradictory reports.
